extracted.intended_audience: researchers, statisticians, grant administrators and policymakers studying peer review reliability and assessor effects
extracted.subtask_short: peer review reliability of grant proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how assessor and researcher attributes affect assessor ratings of grant proposals using a multilevel cross-classified modelling approach; includes measurement of single-rater reliability and investigation of sources of bias (assessor nomination, institutional prestige, assessor workload, researcher rank, assessor origin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-rater reliability of assessor ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously reported single-rater reliabilities have been disappointingly low (between 0.17 and 0.37). In this study the single-rater reliability of the overall assessor rating for Australian Research Council grants was 0.21 for social science and humanities (2870 ratings, 1928 assessors and 687 proposals) and 0.19 for science (7153 ratings, 4295 assessors and 1644 proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: single-rater reliability quantifies how much trust can be placed in an individual assessor's overall rating; values reported here are low, indicating substantial assessor variance and limited reliability of single ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multilevel cross-classified modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: A multilevel, cross-classification approach was used: level 1, assessor and proposal cross-classification; level 2, field of study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modelling guidance: account for the cross-classified structure where assessors rate multiple proposals and proposals are rated by multiple assessors; include higher-level grouping such as field of study. The study explicitly took into account that 34% of the assessors evaluated more than one proposal. This methodology is applicable to other forms of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessor nomination source effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Researcher-nominated assessors (those chosen by the authors of the research proposal) gave higher ratings than panel-nominated assessors chosen by the Australian Research Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation implication: consider potential bias introduced by allowing applicants to nominate assessors; assessor source should be treated as a covariate or controlled in analysis of ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional prestige effect on ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals from more prestigious universities received higher ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note: institutional affiliation/prestige can inflate ratings; analyses of proposal quality or fairness should control for university status when possible to detect and mitigate prestige bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessor origin interacts with institutional prestige (SS&H)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the social sciences and humanities, the status of Australian universities had significantly more effect on Australian assessors than on overseas assessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: assessor country/region of origin moderates how much institutional prestige influences ratings; stratify or test interactions by assessor origin to uncover such differential effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessor workload / number of proposals rated (science)
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, ratings were higher when assessors rated fewer proposals and apparently had a more limited frame of reference for making such ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration: number of proposals assigned to an assessor affects their frame of reference and scoring tendency; workload should be recorded and modelled to avoid conflating workload effects with proposal quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher rank effect (science)
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, ratings were higher when researchers were professors rather than non-professors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation implication: applicant seniority/status (e.g., professor vs non-professor) can bias assessor ratings and should be considered in fairness analyses or controlled for in evaluative models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability of methodology to other peer review contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly, the methodology of this large scale study is applicable to other forms of peer review (publications, job interviews, awarding of prizes and election to prestigious societies) where peer review is employed as a selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: use cross-classified multilevel models and the same attention to assessor/proposal attributes when studying reliability and bias in other peer review settings; treat assessor characteristics, nomination source, workload, and target prestige as candidate predictors.
